solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Rob from Norfolk town gathers groups of friends together (10)

indicators.note: to gather something is to take it in, so DISS holds the groups inside it

blocks.note: Diss is a market town in Norfolk, on the Suffolk border
a posse is a gang of mates

annotation.surface: A thief from a small Norfolk town rounds up gangs of pals for a job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rob from' reads as a nickname, Rob who comes from Norfolk; the definition is the verb to rob, and 'from' only links it to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To dispossess someone is to take their property from them, which is to rob them.

entries.clue: Cast down — just a little (4)

blocks.note: the verb: to hurl something to the ground, or to crush someone's spirits
a noun for a small splash, as of milk in tea

annotation.surface: Someone feeling only slightly glum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast down' looks like an adjective for sad; here it is the verb, to throw down hard.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: to dash is to throw down violently, and a dash is a small splash of something.

entries.clue: One encapsulated by rolling waves lapping edge of shore? (3,4)

definitions.text: One encapsulated by rolling waves lapping edge of shore?

indicators.note: encapsulated means enclosed, so I sits inside the other letters
rolling waves tumble over, so their letters are rearranged
waves lap round the shore, so they wrap the E
the edge of a word is its end, here the final letter of shore

blocks.note: I = one, the Roman numeral
anagram fodder
the last letter of shorE

annotation.surface: A holidaymaker gazing at waves rolling in on the beach.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: waves lapping the shore are exactly what a room with a sea view takes in.
annotation.definitionFit: A sea view is an outlook over the sea, the rolling waves and shoreline in the picture.

entries.clue: Blasts of air finished game (12)

blocks.note: over = ended, as in 'the game is over'
draughts is the British name for checkers

annotation.surface: Someone blowing off steam once the match has ended.
annotation.walkthrough: An overdraught is a current of air passing over something, such as over a fire in a furnace.
annotation.definitionFit: Overdraughts are currents of air blown across the top of a fire or kiln, so blasts of air.

entries.clue: Silence present helpers largely set aside (6)

indicators.note: largely means mostly, so all but the last letter of ELVES is kept

blocks.note: sh! is the call for quiet
ELVES, Santa's present-making helpers, losing the final S

annotation.surface: Quieting Santa's workshop and putting the helpers to one side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like here-and-now; it is a gift, so the helpers are Father Christmas's elves.
annotation.definitionFit: To shelve a plan is to put it aside for later, as if placed on a shelf.

entries.clue: With following wind in last flight (8)

indicators.note: following means coming after, so W comes after AIR
in means inside, so AIR and W are placed inside the word for last

blocks.note: to last is to endure or stay; AIRW goes between ST and AY
wind is moving air
W = with, a standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A plane on its final leg, helped home by a tailwind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Last flight' reads as a final plane journey; 'last' is the verb to endure, and a flight is a set of stairs.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its building sense: a flight is a continuous run of steps between landings, not an air journey.

entries.clue: European chap transmitted message out of America (4)

indicators.note: the A is taken out of the word

blocks.note: an email is a message sent electronically
A = America, a standard abbreviation; it is removed

annotation.surface: A European man sending a note from across the Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'European' looks like it supplies an E; it belongs with 'chap' in the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Emil is a man's name common in Germany, Scandinavia and central Europe.

entries.clue: Masters receiving mortarboard for one sage (7)

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so the two MAs hold HAT

blocks.note: two MAs, Masters of Arts, with HAT going between them
a mortarboard is a type of hat, the square academic cap

annotation.surface: Graduates at a ceremony in academic caps.
annotation.walkthrough: The mortarboard goes with the Masters degrees, so the picture hangs together; 'for one' flags the hat as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A mahatma is a revered wise person in India, a sage, as in Mahatma Gandhi.

entries.clue: Being parasitic, one is a success by accident (5,5)

blocks.note: a liver is one who lives, one who is
a fluke is a lucky chance success

annotation.surface: A freeloader who lives off others and only succeeds by luck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Being parasitic' looks like a description of behaviour; it is a noun phrase, a being that is a parasite.
annotation.definitionFit: The liver fluke is a flatworm that lives as a parasite in the livers of sheep and cattle.

entries.clue: Pet cuckoo is tame, welcoming return of experts (7,3)

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters are scrambled
to welcome is to take in, so the scrambled letters hold SECA
returned means sent back, so ACES reads backwards

blocks.note: anagram fodder
aces are experts; reversed to SECA and put inside SIAME…T

annotation.surface: Someone insisting their mad pet is perfectly tame when the specialists come back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pet cuckoo' reads as a caged bird; the pet is the definition and cuckoo only scrambles 'is tame'.
annotation.definitionFit: A Siamese cat is a popular breed of domestic cat, kept as a pet.

entries.clue: Cutting edge of Romany XV? (4)

blocks.note: X read as the Greek letter chi, then V left as itself

annotation.surface: A rugby fifteen of Roma players at the sharp end.
annotation.walkthrough: XV looks like 15, a rugby team; read as letters, X is the Greek chi and V is just V. Chiv is a Romany word for a knife.
annotation.definitionFit: Chiv, from Romany, is slang for a knife or blade, a cutting edge in the Romany tongue.

entries.clue: Puts forward screening method: acceptable protocol for consumption? (5,7)

indicators.note: to screen something is to hide it behind, so TABLES surrounds MANNER

blocks.note: to table a motion is to put it forward for discussion
a manner is a way or method of doing something

annotation.surface: A doctor proposing a screening test for tuberculosis, once called consumption.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screening' and 'consumption' suggest a medical test for TB; consumption here is eating, and screening only wraps one word round another.
annotation.definitionFit: Table manners are the accepted rules of behaviour when eating, a protocol for consuming food.

entries.clue: Way of overcoming pain through separating object and subject (4,4,6)

blocks.note: the phrase for beating physical discomfort by willpower alone
read literally: in philosophy the thinking self is the subject and the material world the object, with a word for 'above' between them

annotation.surface: A philosophy lecture on coping with pain by splitting self from world.
annotation.walkthrough: Philosophers call the thinking mind the subject and the material world the object, so the phrase literally puts one over the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Mind over matter is the use of willpower to overcome physical problems such as pain.

entries.clue: Securely seal straitjacket? (6-4)

blocks.note: to seal goods tightly in plastic film shrunk by heat
whimsically, a wrap put on by a shrink, a psychiatrist

annotation.surface: Tying someone up tight in a straitjacket.
annotation.walkthrough: A shrink is slang for a psychiatrist, and a straitjacket is the wrap from the old asylum; the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: To shrink-wrap is to seal something in tight plastic film.

entries.clue: If upheld, such an appeal would lead to dismissal (6)

definitions.text: If upheld, such an appeal would lead to dismissal

blocks.note: surface: a legal appeal; setter: a fielder's shout to the umpire
surface: a case thrown out; setter: the batsman given out

annotation.surface: A court appeal that, if it succeeds, gets the case thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: The legal language misleads; this is cricket, where fielders shout 'Howzat?' (how's that?) to ask the umpire to give the batsman out.
annotation.definitionFit: Howzat is the cricketers' appeal to the umpire; if upheld, the batsman is dismissed.

entries.clue: Prime minister going round each and every London street (4,4)

indicators.note: PM goes round ALL, holding it inside

blocks.note: PM = Prime Minister; it wraps round the first ALL
all = each one, as in 'a pound all'
every = all

annotation.surface: The PM touring every street in the capital.
annotation.walkthrough: The prime minister fits the scene, since Pall Mall runs near Whitehall and Downing Street.
annotation.definitionFit: Pall Mall is a street in St James's, central London, known for its gentlemen's clubs.

entries.clue: Black mineral providing the exterior for a great hall (8)

indicators.note: B and SILICA form the outside, with A inside

blocks.note: B = black, as on pencils
A stays as itself
silica is silicon dioxide, the mineral in quartz and sand

annotation.surface: Dark stone cladding a grand building.
annotation.walkthrough: The stone and the hall make one scene, a building faced in dark rock.
annotation.definitionFit: A basilica was a large Roman public hall, later a great church built on that plan.

entries.clue: Built-in from dollar, get nickels back (8)

indicators.note: the letters are taken from within the words that follow
back means reading backwards

blocks.note: the run doL LAR GET NIckels, read backwards

annotation.surface: Change from a dollar handed back in nickels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nickels back' looks like change owed; 'back' only turns round the letters sitting across 'dollar, get nickels'.
annotation.definitionFit: Something integral is built in as an essential part of the whole.

entries.clue: Piggy at last escapes extremely secure pens (7)

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter
to pen is to shut in, so TIE shuts S inside

blocks.note: too = excessively, extremely
to tie is to fasten or secure; it pens the S
the last letter of escapeS

annotation.surface: A pig that finally breaks out of pens that looked very secure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pens' suggests a pigsty; it is the verb to enclose. Piggy is a toe, from the nursery rhyme 'This little piggy went to market'.
annotation.definitionFit: Tootsie is baby talk for a toe, and toes are the 'little piggies' of the rhyme.

entries.clue: Get onto English Evangelist about bishop (6)

indicators.note: about means around, so MARK surrounds B

blocks.note: E = English, a standard abbreviation
Mark is one of the four Gospel writers; he goes about B
B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: An English Gospel preacher cornering a bishop.
annotation.walkthrough: The Evangelist and the bishop make a church scene; the answer is about boarding a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from going into a barque, boarding a ship, and now covers getting onto any vessel or plane.

entries.clue: Crown dependency close to nuclear area turning on cabinet (7)

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so the last letter of nuclear
turning round reverses the order, so IOMRA becomes ARMOI

blocks.note: IOM = Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency
the last letter of nucleaR
A = area
re = on, concerning

annotation.surface: Politics: a small island near a nuclear site rounding on the government.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' suggests ministers; it is a piece of furniture. The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, is a Crown dependency: it belongs to the Crown but is not part of the UK.
annotation.definitionFit: An armoire is a tall cupboard or wardrobe, a type of cabinet.

entries.clue: As Charles is no good at all, stop (4,2)

indicators.note: the G is not there, so it is removed
every G goes, not just one

blocks.note: King Charles is the reigning monarch
G = good; both Gs are removed

annotation.surface: A verdict that the King is no good at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a harsh judgement of King Charles; he is simply 'reigning', and that word loses every G.
annotation.definitionFit: To rein in is to check or halt, as a rider stops a horse by pulling the reins.

entries.clue: Enthusiastic earl drinks in fine writer’s advice on strategy (4,5,5)

indicators.note: to drink something is to take it in, so KEENE holds NOW and THIN

blocks.note: keen = eager, enthusiastic
E = earl; KEEN plus E wraps round NOW THIN
in = fashionable, now
fine = thin, as in a fine thread
the writer's = my, from the setter's point of view

annotation.surface: A keen aristocrat drinking in a fine author's words on tactics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer's advice' reads as one phrase, but 'writer's' is wordplay: the setter speaking of himself, so MY. The maxim comes from Sun Tzu's The Art of War.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Know thine enemy' is the classic strategic maxim, advice from the ancient writer Sun Tzu.

entries.clue: Old impressionist wanting last piece mounted (4)

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so DEGAS loses its final letter
in a down clue, mounted means raised up, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: Edgar Degas, the French Impressionist painter
DEGAS without its last letter

annotation.surface: An old Impressionist painting with a missing last piece, hung on the wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Impressionist' could be a mimic; it is the painter Degas. 'Mounted' suits a hung painting but here turns the word upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having lived a long time, as in an aged relative.

entries.clue: Others take forcible control of broadcast (4)

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken on air, so the word is heard not seen

blocks.note: to wrest is to seize by force; the silent W drops away when it is said

annotation.surface: Rebels seizing a radio station.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a coup at a broadcaster; 'broadcast' only says the word is heard.
annotation.definitionFit: The rest means the others, the remaining ones.

entries.clue: Innovative type charged with taking a look around (10)

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the word for taking a look sits on both sides of the charged type

blocks.note: an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge
peering = looking closely; it wraps round ION

annotation.surface: A go-getting inventor charged with investigating something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Innovative type charged' reads like an inventor under arrest; the definition is only 'Innovative', and the charged type is an ion.
annotation.definitionFit: Pioneering work breaks new ground, which is to be innovative.

entries.clue: DJ who promoted many series of changes on radio (4)

indicators.note: on the radio a word is heard, not seen, so the spelling may change

blocks.note: in bell-ringing a peal is a long series of changes, the sequences rung on a set of bells

annotation.surface: A radio DJ who championed many acts and played music through changing times.
annotation.walkthrough: John Peel was the BBC Radio 1 DJ famous for championing new bands; 'on radio' suits him and also says the word is heard.
annotation.definitionFit: John Peel, the BBC disc jockey, promoted countless new bands through his radio sessions.

entries.clue: Warned not to pay, might chap be in danger at work? (10)

indicators.note: ISHE goes in the rearranged letters
letters at work are busy moving about, so DANGER is rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder; ISHE goes inside after GARN
'might chap be…?' asks 'is he…?'

annotation.surface: Someone told to withhold payment wonders if a worker is in peril on the job.
annotation.walkthrough: A garnishee is a person who owes money to a debtor and is legally warned to pay it to the creditor instead; 'might chap be' is the question 'is he?'.
annotation.definitionFit: To garnishee someone is to serve a legal notice ordering them not to pay money to a debtor.
